title: OF THE ACCUMULATION OF CAPITAL, OR OF PRODUCTIVE AND UNPRODUCTIVE LABOUR.
paragraphs: On the Accumulation of Capital, or on Productive and Unproductive Labour

Some kinds of labour add to the value of whatever they are applied to; other kinds do not. The first kind produces value, so we can call it productive; the second kind we can call unproductive. {Some learned and clever French writers have used these terms in a different sense. In the final chapter of Book Four I will try to show that their usage is mistaken.} A manufacturer's labour, for instance, generally adds to the value of the materials he works on: it adds the cost of his own upkeep and his employer's profit. A household servant's labour, by contrast, adds value to nothing. Although the manufacturer has his wages paid in advance by his employer, he actually costs his employer nothing, because the value of those wages is normally recovered, along with a profit, in the increased value of the thing he has worked on. But the cost of keeping a household servant is never recovered. A man grows rich by employing many manufacturers; he grows poor by keeping many servants. Still, the servant's labour has its own value and deserves its reward just as much as the manufacturer's does. The difference is that the manufacturer's labour is fixed and embodied in some specific object or saleable commodity, which lasts for at least a while after the work is finished. It is, in effect, a certain quantity of labour stored up, ready to be put to use again later if needed. That object — or, what amounts to the same thing, its price — can afterwards, if necessary, set in motion an amount of labour equal to what originally produced it. The servant's labour, on the other hand, is not fixed or embodied in any specific object or saleable commodity. His services usually vanish the moment they are performed, and rarely leave behind any trace of value that could later be used to buy an equal amount of service.

The labour of some of the most respected groups in society is, like that of household servants, unproductive of any value. It does not fix or embody itself in any lasting object or saleable commodity that survives after the work is done and could later purchase an equal amount of labour. The sovereign, for example, together with all the officers of justice and of war who serve under him, and the entire army and navy, are all unproductive labourers. They are servants of the public, supported out of a portion of the annual produce of other people's industry. However honourable, useful, or necessary their service may be, it produces nothing that could later buy an equal amount of service in return. The protection, security, and defence of the nation, which their work provides this year, will not purchase next year's protection, security, and defence. Into this same category fall some of the gravest and most important professions, as well as some of the most frivolous ones: clergymen, lawyers, physicians, and writers of every sort, along with actors, clowns, musicians, opera singers, opera dancers, and the like. The labour of the lowliest of these has a definite value, set by exactly the same principles that govern every other kind of labour; and the labour of the noblest and most useful among them produces nothing that could afterwards buy or procure an equal amount of labour. Like the actor's lines, the orator's speech, or the musician's tune, the work of all of them perishes at the very instant it is produced.

Productive labourers, unproductive labourers, and people who do no work at all are all alike supported by the annual produce of the country's land and labour. However great this produce may be, it can never be infinite; it always has definite limits. So depending on whether a smaller or larger share of it is used in any given year to support unproductive people, more or less will be left for productive people, and next year's produce will be correspondingly larger or smaller. For with the exception of what the earth yields spontaneously, the entire annual produce is the result of productive labour.

The whole annual produce of every country's land and labour is, of course, ultimately meant to supply the inhabitants' consumption and to provide them with an income. Yet when it first comes either out of the ground or from the hands of the productive labourers, it naturally splits into two parts. One part — often the larger — is first set aside to replace a capital, that is, to renew the provisions, materials, and finished goods that had been drawn out of a capital. The other part forms an income, either for the owner of that capital, as the profit on his stock, or for someone else, as the rent on his land. So with the produce of land, one part replaces the farmer's capital while the other pays his profit and the landlord's rent, thus forming an income both for the owner of the capital, as profit on his stock, and for another person, as rent on his land. In the same way, with the produce of a large factory, one part — always the larger — replaces the capital of the person running the enterprise, while the other pays his profit and so forms an income for the owner of that capital.

The portion of any country's annual produce that replaces a capital is never used directly to support anyone but productive workers. It pays only the wages of productive labour. The portion meant directly to form an income, whether as profit or as rent, can support either productive or unproductive people indifferently.

Whenever a man uses part of his stock as a capital, he always expects it to come back to him with a profit. So he uses it only to support productive workers; and after it has served him as a capital, it becomes an income for them. Whenever he uses any part of it to support unproductive people of any kind, that part is from that moment withdrawn from his capital and shifted into the stock he keeps for immediate consumption.

Unproductive labourers, and those who do no work at all, are all supported out of income. They are supported either, first, by the part of the annual produce originally meant to form an income for particular people, whether as land rent or as profit on stock; or, second, by the part that, although originally meant to replace a capital and support only productive workers, can — once it reaches their hands — be used, in whatever portion exceeds their necessary subsistence, to support either productive or unproductive people indifferently. So not only the great landlord or the rich merchant, but even the ordinary workman, if his wages are sizeable, can keep a household servant; or he may sometimes go to a play or a puppet show, and so do his bit toward supporting one set of unproductive labourers; or he may pay some taxes, and so help support another set, more honourable and useful, but equally unproductive. No part of the annual produce originally meant to replace a capital, however, is ever channelled toward supporting unproductive people until after it has set in motion its full quota of productive labour — all that it could set in motion in the way it was being used. The workman must first have earned his wages by work done before he can spend any of them this way. And that part is usually only a small one. It is only his spare income, of which productive labourers rarely have much. Still, they generally have some; and when it comes to paying taxes, their sheer numbers may to some extent make up for the smallness of each contribution. Land rent and profit on stock are therefore everywhere the main sources from which unproductive people draw their subsistence. These are the two kinds of income whose owners generally have the most to spare. Both could support either productive or unproductive people indifferently — yet they seem to have a certain preference for the unproductive. A great lord's spending generally feeds more idle people than industrious ones. The rich merchant, though with his capital he supports only industrious people, through his spending — that is, through how he uses his income — commonly feeds the very same sort of people the great lord does.

The ratio between productive and unproductive people in any country therefore depends heavily on the ratio between two parts of the annual produce: the part that, as soon as it comes out of the ground or from the productive labourers' hands, is meant to replace a capital, and the part meant to form an income, whether as rent or as profit. This ratio is very different in rich countries from what it is in poor ones.

Today, in the wealthy countries of Europe, a very large share of the produce of land — often the largest — is meant to replace the capital of the rich and independent farmer; the rest pays his profits and the landlord's rent. But in earlier times, when feudal government prevailed, only a very small share of the produce was needed to replace the capital used in farming. That capital usually consisted of a few miserable cattle, kept entirely on the land's spontaneous growth on uncultivated ground, and so it could itself be counted as part of that spontaneous growth. It generally belonged to the landlord too, and he advanced it to those who worked the land. All the rest of the produce properly belonged to him as well, either as rent for his land or as profit on this paltry capital. Those who worked the land were generally serfs, whose persons and possessions were equally his property. Those who were not serfs were tenants-at-will; and although the rent they paid was often nominally little more than a token quit-rent, it really amounted to the whole produce of the land. Their lord could at any time command their labour in peacetime and their service in war. Even though they lived away from his house, they depended on him just as much as the retainers who lived in it. But the whole produce of the land undoubtedly belongs to the man who can dispose of the labour and service of everyone the land supports. In the present state of Europe, the landlord's share rarely exceeds a third, and sometimes is no more than a fourth, of the whole produce of the land. Yet land rent, in all the improved parts of the country, has been tripled and quadrupled since those ancient times; so this third or fourth of the annual produce is apparently three or four times greater than the whole had been before. As improvement advances, rent rises in proportion to the extent of land but falls in proportion to its produce.

In the wealthy countries of Europe, large capitals are now employed in trade and manufacturing. In the old days, the little trade that went on, and the few crude and homely manufactures that were carried out, needed only very small capitals. These must, however, have yielded very large profits. The rate of interest was nowhere lower than ten percent, and their profits must have been high enough to cover this steep interest. Today, in the improved parts of Europe, the rate of interest is nowhere higher than six percent, and in some of the most improved areas it is as low as four, three, or even two percent. The part of the inhabitants' income that comes from profit on stock is always far greater in rich countries than in poor ones, but that is because the stock is far greater; in proportion to the stock, the profits are generally much smaller.

So the part of the annual produce that, as soon as it comes out of the ground or from the productive labourers' hands, is meant to replace a capital, is not only much greater in rich countries than in poor ones; it also makes up a much greater proportion of the produce than the part meant directly to form an income as rent or profit. The funds meant to support productive labour are not only much greater in rich countries than in poor ones, but make up a much larger share relative to the funds that — though they could support either productive or unproductive people — generally have a preference for the unproductive.

The ratio between these different funds necessarily determines, in every country, the general character of its people as to industry or idleness. We are more industrious than our forefathers, because nowadays the funds meant to support industry are much greater, relative to those likely to be spent on idleness, than they were two or three centuries ago. Our ancestors were idle because there was not enough encouragement to be industrious. As the proverb says, it is better to play for nothing than to work for nothing. In trading and manufacturing towns, where the lower ranks of people are mainly supported by the use of capital, they are generally industrious, sober, and prosperous — as in many English and most Dutch towns. In towns supported mainly by the regular or occasional presence of a court, where the lower ranks are mainly supported by the spending of income, the people are generally idle, dissolute, and poor — as at Rome, Versailles, Compiègne, and Fontainebleau. Apart from Rouen and Bordeaux, there is little trade or industry in any of the parliament towns of France; and the lower ranks there, being supported mainly by the spending of the members of the law courts and of those who come to plead before them, are generally idle and poor. The great trade of Rouen and Bordeaux seems to be entirely the result of their location. Rouen is necessarily the depot for almost all the goods brought either from foreign countries or from the coastal provinces of France for consumption in the great city of Paris. Bordeaux, likewise, is the depot for the wines grown on the banks of the Garonne and of the rivers feeding into it — one of the richest wine regions in the world, which seems to produce the wine best suited for export, or best matched to foreign tastes. Such advantageous locations necessarily attract a great capital by the great employment they offer it, and the use of this capital is what makes those two cities industrious. In the other parliament towns of France, very little more capital seems to be used than is needed to supply their own consumption — that is, little more than the smallest capital that can be used there. The same can be said of Paris, Madrid, and Vienna. Of those three cities, Paris is by far the most industrious, but Paris itself is the chief market for all the manufactures established in Paris, and its own consumption is the main object of all the trade it carries on. London, Lisbon, and Copenhagen are perhaps the only three cities in Europe that are both the constant residence of a court and can at the same time count as trading cities — cities that trade not only for their own consumption but for that of other cities and countries. The location of all three is extremely advantageous, and naturally fits them to be depots for a great part of the goods meant for consumption in distant places. In a city where a great income is spent, it is probably harder to employ a capital profitably for any purpose other than supplying that city's own consumption than it is in a city where the lower ranks of people have no other livelihood than what they get from employing such a capital. The idleness of most of the people supported by the spending of income probably corrupts the industry of those who ought to be supported by the use of capital, and makes it less profitable to employ a capital there than elsewhere. There was little trade or industry in Edinburgh before the Union. Once the Scottish parliament no longer met there, and once it ceased to be the necessary residence of the principal nobility and gentry of Scotland, it became a city of some trade and industry. It still remains, however, the seat of the chief law courts of Scotland, of the boards of customs and excise, and so on. So a considerable income is still spent there. In trade and industry it is far inferior to Glasgow, whose people are mainly supported by the use of capital. It has sometimes been observed that the people of a large village, after making considerable progress in manufactures, have become idle and poor because some great lord took up residence in their neighbourhood.

So the ratio between capital and income seems everywhere to govern the ratio between industry and idleness. Wherever capital predominates, industry prevails; wherever income predominates, idleness prevails. Every increase or decrease of capital therefore naturally tends to increase or decrease the real amount of industry, the number of productive workers, and consequently the exchangeable value of the annual produce of the country's land and labour — the real wealth and income of all its inhabitants.
Capital is increased by thrift, and reduced by extravagance and mismanagement.

Whatever a person saves out of his income he adds to his capital. He then either uses it himself to support an additional number of productive workers, or enables someone else to do so by lending it to him at interest — that is, for a share of the profits. Just as an individual's capital can be increased only by what he saves out of his annual income or annual gains, so a society's capital — which is simply the sum of all its members' capitals — can be increased only in the same way.

Thrift, not industry, is the immediate cause of the increase of capital. Industry does provide the material that thrift accumulates; but whatever industry might acquire, if thrift did not save and store it up, the capital would never grow.

By increasing the fund meant to support productive workers, thrift tends to increase the number of workers whose labour adds to the value of whatever it is applied to. So it tends to increase the exchangeable value of the annual produce of the country's land and labour. It sets in motion an additional amount of industry, which adds value to the annual produce.

What is saved each year is consumed just as regularly as what is spent each year, and at nearly the same time too — but it is consumed by a different set of people. The portion of his income that a rich man spends each year is, in most cases, consumed by idle guests and household servants, who leave nothing behind in return for what they consume. The portion he saves each year is, for the sake of the profit, immediately put to use as a capital, and so is consumed in the same way and at nearly the same time — but by a different set of people: by labourers, manufacturers, and craftsmen, who reproduce, with a profit, the value of what they consume each year. Suppose his income is paid to him in money. Had he spent the whole of it, the food, clothing, and lodging it could have bought would have been distributed among the first set of people. By saving a part of it — since that part is, for the sake of the profit, immediately used as a capital, either by himself or by someone else — the food, clothing, and lodging it can buy are necessarily set aside for the second set. The consumption is the same, but the consumers are different.

Through what a thrifty man saves each year, he not only provides support for an additional number of productive workers for the coming year; like the founder of a public workhouse, he in effect sets up a permanent fund to support an equal number of workers in all times to come. The permanent earmarking of this fund for that purpose is not always protected by any actual law, by any trust or deed of perpetual ownership. But it is always protected by a very powerful principle: the plain and obvious self-interest of every individual to whom any share of it will ever belong. No part of it can ever afterwards be used to support anyone but productive workers without an obvious loss to whoever thus diverts it from its proper purpose.

This is how the spendthrift diverts it. By not keeping his spending within his income, he eats into his capital. Like a man who diverts the revenues of some pious foundation to worldly purposes, he pays the wages of idleness with funds that his forefathers' thrift had, in effect, consecrated to the support of industry. By reducing the funds meant for productive labour, he necessarily reduces — so far as it depends on him — the amount of that labour which adds value to whatever it is applied to, and consequently the value of the annual produce of the whole country's land and labour, the real wealth and income of its inhabitants. If the extravagance of some were not offset by the thrift of others, the conduct of every spendthrift, by feeding the idle with the bread of the industrious, would tend not only to beggar himself but to impoverish his country.

Even if the spendthrift's spending were entirely on home-made goods and none on foreign goods, its effect on the society's productive funds would still be the same. Every year there would still be a certain amount of food and clothing — which ought to have supported productive people — used instead to support unproductive people. So every year there would still be some reduction in what would otherwise have been the value of the annual produce of the country's land and labour.

It may be said, true enough, that since this spending is not on foreign goods and causes no export of gold and silver, the same quantity of money would stay in the country as before. But if the food and clothing thus consumed by unproductive people had instead been distributed among productive people, they would have reproduced, along with a profit, the full value of what they consumed. In that case the same quantity of money would equally have stayed in the country, and on top of that there would have been a reproduction of an equal value of consumable goods. There would have been two values instead of one.

Besides, the same quantity of money cannot stay long in any country where the value of the annual produce is falling. The sole use of money is to circulate consumable goods. By means of money, provisions, materials, and finished work are bought, sold, and distributed to their proper consumers. So the quantity of money that can be used in any country each year must be determined by the value of the consumable goods circulated within it each year. Those goods must consist either in the immediate produce of the country's own land and labour, or in something bought with part of that produce. Their value, then, must fall as the value of that produce falls, and with it the quantity of money that can be used to circulate them. But the money that this annual fall in produce annually pushes out of domestic circulation will not be left to sit idle. Whoever owns it has an interest in putting it to use; and having no use for it at home, it will — in spite of all laws and prohibitions — be sent abroad and used to buy consumable goods that may be of some use at home. Its annual export will in this way keep adding something, for a while, to the country's annual consumption beyond the value of its own annual produce. What was saved out of the annual produce in the days of prosperity, and used to buy gold and silver, will help support consumption in adversity for a little while. The export of gold and silver, in this case, is not the cause but the effect of the country's decline, and may even, for a short time, ease the misery of that decline.

Conversely, the quantity of money in every country must naturally rise as the value of the annual produce rises. With a greater value of consumable goods circulating within the society each year, more money will be needed to circulate them. So part of the increased produce will naturally be used to buy, wherever it can be had, the additional gold and silver needed to circulate the rest. In this case the increase of those metals is the effect, not the cause, of the nation's prosperity. Gold and silver are bought everywhere in the same way. The food, clothing, and lodging — the income and upkeep — of all those whose labour or stock is employed in bringing them from the mine to the market is the price paid for them in Peru just as in England. The country that has this price to pay will never be long without the quantity of those metals it has need of, and no country will ever long hold on to a quantity it has no need of.

So whatever we may imagine a country's real wealth and income to consist of — whether in the value of the annual produce of its land and labour, as plain reason seems to suggest, or in the quantity of precious metals circulating within it, as common prejudice supposes — either way, every spendthrift appears as a public enemy, and every thrifty man as a public benefactor.

The effects of mismanagement are often the same as those of extravagance. Every ill-judged and unsuccessful venture in farming, mining, fishing, trade, or manufacturing tends in the same way to reduce the funds meant to support productive labour. In every such venture, even though the capital is consumed only by productive workers, the ill-judged way they are employed means they do not reproduce the full value of what they consume; so there must always be some reduction in what would otherwise have been the society's productive funds.

It can seldom happen, in fact, that a great nation's circumstances are much affected either by the extravagance or the mismanagement of individuals; the wastefulness or imprudence of some is always more than offset by the thrift and good conduct of others.

As for extravagance: the impulse that prompts spending is the craving for present enjoyment, which, though sometimes violent and very hard to control, is generally only momentary and occasional. But the impulse that prompts saving is the desire to better our condition — a desire that, though generally calm and undramatic, is with us from the womb and never leaves us until we go to the grave. In the whole stretch between those two moments there is hardly a single instance, perhaps, of a man so perfectly and completely satisfied with his situation as to wish for no change or improvement of any kind. For most men, the way they propose and hope to better their condition is by increasing their fortune. It is the most ordinary and obvious means; and the likeliest way to increase a fortune is to save and accumulate part of what one acquires, either regularly each year or on some special occasion. So although the impulse to spend prevails in nearly all men on some occasions, and in some men on nearly all occasions, in most men, taking their whole life on average, the impulse to thrift seems not only to predominate but to predominate by a wide margin.

As for mismanagement: the number of prudent and successful undertakings is everywhere far greater than the number of ill-judged and unsuccessful ones. For all our complaints about how often bankruptcies happen, the unfortunate men who suffer this calamity make up only a very small part of the whole number engaged in trade and in every other kind of business — perhaps not much more than one in a thousand. Bankruptcy is perhaps the greatest and most humiliating disaster that can befall an honest man. So most men are careful enough to avoid it. Some, it is true, do not avoid it — just as some do not avoid the gallows.

Great nations are never impoverished by private extravagance or mismanagement, though they sometimes are by public ones. In most countries, the whole or nearly the whole of the public revenue is spent on supporting unproductive people. These are the people who make up a numerous and splendid court, a great church establishment, and great fleets and armies — who in peacetime produce nothing, and in wartime acquire nothing that can offset the cost of supporting them, even while the war lasts. Since such people produce nothing themselves, they are all supported by the produce of other men's labour. So when they are multiplied beyond what is needed, they may in a particular year consume so large a share of this produce as to leave too little to support the productive labourers who should reproduce it the next year. Next year's produce will therefore be smaller than this year's; and if the same disorder continues, the third year's produce will be smaller still than the second's. These unproductive people, who ought to be supported by only a part of the people's spare income, may consume so large a share of their whole income, and thereby force so many people to eat into their capital — into the funds meant to support productive labour — that all the thrift and good conduct of individuals may not be able to offset the waste and degradation of produce caused by this violent and forced encroachment.

Yet this thrift and good conduct is, on most occasions, experience shows, enough to offset not only the private extravagance and mismanagement of individuals but the public extravagance of government too. The steady, constant, and uninterrupted effort of every man to better his condition — the very source from which public and national wealth, as well as private wealth, originally springs — is often powerful enough to keep things naturally progressing toward improvement, in spite both of the extravagance of government and of the greatest errors of administration. Like the mysterious principle of animal life, it often restores health and vigour to the body in spite not only of the disease but of the absurd prescriptions of the doctor.

The annual produce of any nation's land and labour can be raised in value only by raising either the number of its productive labourers or the productive power of the labourers already employed. The number of productive labourers, clearly, can never be much increased except by an increase of capital — of the funds meant to support them. And the productive power of the same number of labourers cannot be increased except by some addition or improvement to the machines and tools that ease and shorten labour, or by a better division and distribution of the work. In either case, an additional capital is almost always required. Only by means of additional capital can the person running an enterprise either provide his workers with better machinery or arrange a better division of work among them. When the work to be done consists of many parts, keeping every man constantly employed in one part requires a much greater capital than when every man is occasionally employed in every different part. So when we compare a nation's state at two different periods, and find that the annual produce of its land and labour is plainly greater in the later period than in the earlier one — its lands better cultivated, its manufactures more numerous and flourishing, its trade more extensive — we may be sure that its capital must have increased over the interval between those periods, and that more must have been added to it by the good conduct of some than was taken from it by the private mismanagement of others or the public extravagance of government. And we shall find this to have been the case with almost all nations in all reasonably quiet and peaceable times, even those that have not enjoyed the most prudent and thrifty governments. To judge this rightly, though, we must compare the state of the country at periods somewhat far apart. The progress is often so gradual that, over short intervals, the improvement is not only not noticeable but, because of the decline either of certain branches of industry or of certain districts — things that sometimes happen even when the country as a whole is very prosperous — there often arises a suspicion that the wealth and industry of the whole are decaying.

The annual produce of England's land and labour, for instance, is certainly far greater than it was a little over a century ago, at the Restoration of Charles II. Although few people today, I believe, doubt this, during that period scarcely five years have passed without some book or pamphlet appearing — and written, too, with enough skill to gain some authority with the public — claiming to prove that the nation's wealth was rapidly declining: that the country was being depopulated, agriculture neglected, manufactures decaying, and trade ruined. Nor have all these publications been party pamphlets, the wretched offspring of falsehood and corruption. Many were written by very honest and very intelligent people, who wrote nothing but what they believed, and for no other reason than that they believed it.

Again, the annual produce of England's land and labour was certainly far greater at the Restoration than we can suppose it to have been about a hundred years earlier, at the accession of Elizabeth. At that earlier time, too, we have every reason to believe, the country was much further advanced in improvement than it had been about a century before that, toward the close of the conflicts between the houses of York and Lancaster. Even then it was probably in a better condition than it had been at the Norman Conquest; and at the Norman Conquest, better than during the chaos of the Saxon heptarchy. Even at that early date it was certainly a more improved country than at the invasion of Julius Caesar, when its inhabitants were in nearly the same state as the savages in North America.

In each of these periods, however, there was not only much private and public wastefulness, many expensive and needless wars, and a great diversion of the annual produce from supporting productive people to supporting unproductive ones; but sometimes, amid the chaos of civil strife, there was such utter waste and destruction of stock as might be supposed not only to slow down — as it certainly did — the natural accumulation of riches, but to have left the country poorer at the end of the period than at the beginning. So in the happiest and most fortunate of all these periods, the one since the Restoration, how many disorders and misfortunes have occurred which, had they been foreseen, would have been expected to bring not just impoverishment but the total ruin of the country: the Fire and the Plague of London, the two Dutch wars, the disorders of the Revolution, the war in Ireland, the four expensive French wars of 1688, 1701, 1742, and 1756, together with the two rebellions of 1715 and 1745. In the course of the four French wars the nation has run up more than £145,000,000 of debt, over and above all the other extraordinary annual expense they caused, so that the whole cannot be reckoned at less than £200,000,000. So large a share of the annual produce of the country's land and labour has, since the Revolution, been used on various occasions to support an extraordinary number of unproductive people. But had those wars not given this particular direction to so large a capital, most of it would naturally have been used to support productive people, whose labour would have replaced, with a profit, the whole value of what they consumed. The value of the annual produce of the country's land and labour would have been considerably increased by it every year, and every year's increase would have increased still further that of the following year. More houses would have been built, more land improved, and land already improved better cultivated; more manufactures would have been set up, and those already set up extended further; and how high the real wealth and income of the country might by now have risen, it is perhaps not very easy even to imagine.

But although the wastefulness of government must certainly have slowed England's natural progress toward wealth and improvement, it has not been able to stop it. The annual produce of its land and labour is undoubtedly far greater now than it was at either the Restoration or the Revolution. So the capital employed each year in cultivating this land and supporting this labour must likewise be far greater. In the midst of all the government's exactions, this capital has been silently and gradually accumulated by the private thrift and good conduct of individuals, through their universal, continual, and uninterrupted effort to better their own condition. It is this effort — protected by law, and allowed by liberty to exert itself in the most advantageous way — that has kept England progressing toward wealth and improvement in almost all past times, and that, it is to be hoped, will keep it doing so in all future times. England, however, having never been blessed with a very thrifty government, has at no time had thrift as the characteristic virtue of its inhabitants. So it is the height of impertinence and presumption in kings and ministers to pretend to oversee the economy of private people, and to restrain their spending either by sumptuary laws or by banning the import of foreign luxuries. They are themselves always, and without exception, the greatest spendthrifts in the society. Let them look well after their own spending, and they may safely trust private people with theirs. If their own extravagance does not ruin the state, that of their subjects never will.

Just as thrift increases the public capital and extravagance reduces it, so the conduct of those whose spending exactly matches their income — neither accumulating nor encroaching — neither increases nor reduces it. Some modes of spending, however, seem to contribute more to the growth of public wealth than others.

An individual's income may be spent either on things that are consumed immediately — where one day's spending can neither lighten nor support the cost of the next — or on more durable things, which can therefore be accumulated, and where each day's spending may, as he chooses, either lighten or support and heighten the effect of the next day's. A man of fortune, for example, may either spend his income on a lavish and extravagant table and on keeping a great number of household servants and a host of dogs and horses; or, content with a modest table and few attendants, he may lay out most of it on adorning his house or country villa, on useful or ornamental buildings, on useful or ornamental furniture, on collecting books, statues, and pictures; or on more frivolous things — jewels, baubles, ingenious trinkets of various kinds; or, most trifling of all, on amassing a great wardrobe of fine clothes, like the favourite and minister of a great prince who died a few years ago. If two men of equal fortune were to spend their incomes, the one chiefly in the first way and the other chiefly in the second, the magnificence of the man who spent chiefly on durable goods would keep growing, each day's spending adding something to support and heighten the effect of the next day's; while that of the other would be no greater at the end of the period than at the beginning. The first man, too, would be the richer of the two at the end of the period. He would have a stock of goods of some kind, which, though it might not be worth all it cost, would always be worth something. Of the second man's spending, no trace or vestige would remain, and the effects of ten or twenty years' wastefulness would be as completely wiped out as if they had never existed.

Just as one mode of spending is more favourable than the other to an individual's wealth, so it is to a nation's. The houses, furniture, and clothing of the rich, before long, become useful to the lower and middle ranks of people. They can buy them when their superiors grow tired of them; and so the general comfort of the whole people is gradually improved, once this mode of spending becomes common among men of fortune. In countries that have long been rich, you will often find the lower ranks of people possessing houses and furniture that are perfectly good and intact, but which neither could have been built nor made for their use. What was once a seat of the Seymour family is now an inn on the Bath road. The marriage bed of James I of Great Britain, which his queen brought with her from Denmark as a gift fit for one sovereign to give another, was a few years ago the showpiece of an alehouse at Dunfermline. In some ancient cities, which have either long stood still or somewhat decayed, you will sometimes scarcely find a single house that could have been built for its present inhabitants. And if you go into those houses, you will often find many excellent, though old-fashioned, pieces of furniture, still very fit for use, which could as little have been made for them. Noble palaces, magnificent villas, and great collections of books, statues, and pictures, and other rarities, are often both an ornament and an honour, not only to their neighbourhood but to the whole country they belong to. Versailles is an ornament and an honour to France, Stowe and Wilton to England. Italy still commands a certain reverence for the number of such monuments it possesses, even though the wealth that produced them has decayed and the genius that designed them seems to have died out — perhaps for want of the same employment.

Spending on durable goods is favourable not only to accumulation but to thrift. If a person should ever overspend on it, he can easily cut back without exposing himself to public censure. To reduce his servants drastically, to scale his table back from great extravagance to great frugality, to give up his carriage and horses once he has set them up — these are changes that cannot escape his neighbours' notice, and that are taken to imply some admission of past bad conduct. So few of those once unfortunate enough to have plunged too far into this kind of spending afterwards have the courage to reform, until ruin and bankruptcy force them to. But if a person has at any time spent too much on building, furniture, books, or pictures, no imprudence can be inferred from a change in his conduct. These are things in which further spending is often made unnecessary by past spending; so when a person stops, he appears to do so not because he has overshot his fortune but because he has satisfied his taste.

Spending on durable goods, besides, commonly supports a greater number of people than spending on the most lavish hospitality. Of the two or three hundredweight of provisions sometimes served up at a great feast, perhaps half is thrown to the dunghill, and there is always a great deal wasted and abused. But if the cost of this entertainment had been used to set masons, carpenters, upholsterers, mechanics, and the like to work, a quantity of provisions of equal value would have been distributed among an even greater number of people, who would have bought them in pennyworths and pound-weights, and not lost or thrown away a single ounce. In the one way, besides, this spending supports productive people; in the other, unproductive ones. So in the one way it increases, and in the other it does not increase, the exchangeable value of the annual produce of the country's land and labour.

I would not, however, by all this, be understood to mean that the one kind of spending always signals a more generous or open-handed spirit than the other. When a man of fortune spends his income chiefly on hospitality, he shares most of it with his friends and companions; but when he uses it to buy such durable goods, he often spends the whole on himself and gives nothing to anyone without getting an equivalent in return. So the latter kind of spending, especially when aimed at frivolous objects — the little ornaments of dress and furniture, jewels, trinkets, gewgaws — often reveals not just a trifling disposition but a mean and selfish one. All I mean is that the one kind of spending, since it always brings about some accumulation of valuable goods, since it is more favourable to private thrift and therefore to the increase of the public capital, and since it supports productive rather than unproductive people, contributes more than the other to the growth of public wealth.
